Pima (Akimel O'odham)

Akimel O’odham, often encountered under the historical reading label Pima, should not be reduced to one present government. Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community and Gila River Indian Community publish distinct accounts of their O’odham and Piipaash/Pee Posh communities. Together with an irrigation education lesson, they provide starting points for farming, water loss and community history.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Identity and context

Akimel O’odham is a people’s name encountered alongside Pima. The Gila River Indian Community includes distinct constituent peoples.

Read the sources [1] Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: River relationships, language and community-specific history. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community [2] Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community [3] Pima-Maricopa Irrigation Project, Education Initiative

03

Read particular communities within a broader label

The Salt River and Gila River accounts each identify distinct O’odham and Piipaash/Pee Posh peoples within a particular community. Their histories are related reading routes, not interchangeable government names or evidence that all these peoples are one group. Keep the speaker and community scope attached to each account.

Read the sources [1] Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community [4] Gila River Indian Community

04

Farming and the loss of river water

The community histories and irrigation lesson connect farming with river water and describe the consequences of diversion. The lesson is especially useful for an introductory account of water loss, but its future-looking project language belongs to the document’s own period. It does not establish that later irrigation plans were completed or resolve present legal rights.

Read the sources [1] Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community [3] Pima-Maricopa Irrigation Project, Education Initiative [4] Gila River Indian Community

05

Archaeology and community accounts need context

The education lesson distinguishes archaeological interpretations from community histories and asks readers to consider where interpretations differ. Labels such as Hohokam should therefore be read within their scholarly and community contexts, not used as proof that a people vanished or as an automatic identity assignment. The underlying archaeological works require separate inspection.

Read the sources [3] Pima-Maricopa Irrigation Project, Education Initiative [1] Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community

History | Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community ↗

A Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community history introduces its distinct O’odham and Piipaash peoples, farming and the consequences of river diversion. It is one government/community perspective within a wider Akimel O’odham reading route.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual main History body, ordinary web-reader lines 49–71: two distinct peoples, community history, archaeology/ancestry interpretation, irrigation and diversion. The timeline included farther down the page overlaps p293-s2 and is not counted again.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual selected public content inspected on 2026-10-28. No access bypass or outreach. Linked media are not cleared by this textual review. Normal HTTP 200 redirected www to non-www; inherited ID and original URL retained. Archaeological labels are not treated as vanished ethnic groups or automatic proof of a single descent line. Present legal boundaries, totals and current project outcomes are not established.

https://www.srpmic-nsn.gov/about/history/

Pima-Maricopa Irrigation Project, Education Initiative ↗

A Pima-Maricopa Irrigation Project education lesson introduces Akimel O’otham and Pee Posh histories and water loss. Read its historical overview and its distinction between archaeological interpretations and community memory.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual extracted text of all four PDF pages inspected. Selected use: p.1 opening identifies two distinct peoples; p.2 farming/water-loss narrative; p.3 educational objectives and the explicit limits of archaeological agreement. The p.4 chart was text-extracted, not visually rendered.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual selected public content inspected on 2026-10-28. No access bypass or outreach. Linked media are not cleared by this textual review. Four-page PDF normally retrieved HTTP 200. Undated legacy lesson includes future-looking irrigation/settlement language; no project completion or current acreage is asserted. Underlying quotations and archaeological publications were not inspected. No full visual chart inspection claimed.

https://www.gilariver.com/lessons/waterlosslesson01.pdf

Indigenous-ledGila River Indian CommunitySource 4

History — Gila River Indian Community perspective ↗

The Community’s historical account connects its Akimel O’otham and Pee Posh peoples with farming, irrigation and the effects of river diversion. It complements rather than replaces the separate Salt River account.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual substantial main History body: community self-description, irrigation/agriculture, selected colonial-observer narrative and water loss. Conflicting/qualified arrival chronology and future-looking irrigation plans were read but not adopted as settled/current facts.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Actual selected public content inspected on 2026-10-28. No access bypass or outreach. Linked media are not cleared by this textual review. This is a particular community perspective, not all Pima-speaking people or proof that Pee Posh are the same people. Original colonial texts were not inspected. Future-looking project language is treated as legacy; no current irrigation outcome, legal entitlement or boundary is inferred.

https://www.gilariver.org/index.php/about/history
